ITID-51111.def: A data-breach-context leaf capturing incidents where credential material was extracted via password-dumping techniques (e.g. from memory, SAM/NTDS.dit, or a password manager/database) and the resulting exposure is the object of concern, rather than the dumping technique's forensic detail.
ITID-51111.purpose: Provides an intake/cross-reference point for password-dumping activity when the classification need is 'this led to a data breach' rather than the technical mechanics of the dump itself.
scopeIncludes: Initial triage of a suspected credential dump before the specific dumping method is confirmed
Cases where the breach angle (what credentials were exposed, who is affected) matters more than the intrusion mechanics
Incidents reported by a third party as 'password dump' without technical detail yet available
scopeExcludes: Confirmed in-memory or database-level password dumping mechanics (see ITID-12133 and the ITID-127xx credential-access series for full technical treatment)
Credentials obtained via phishing rather than dumping (ITID-51121)
Credential stuffing using previously dumped credentials (ITID-51131)
ITID-51111.severity: High. Any confirmed password dump implies broad credential exposure across potentially many accounts.
ITID-51111.priority: P1 while scope is undetermined; re-triage to the specific technical ITID once the dumping method is confirmed.
ITID-51111.escalation: Escalate immediately to the incident commander and identity/security engineering; treat as a mass credential-reset event until scope is bounded.
indicators: Unexplained LSASS, SAM, or NTDS.dit access
A password-manager or credential-store export event with no legitimate business reason
Third-party or law-enforcement notification referencing a 'password dump'
vectors: Memory-resident credential dumping tools
Direct extraction from a credential database or vault
Theft of an unencrypted password export/backup file
rootCauses: Inadequate LSASS/credential-store protection
Unencrypted credential exports left accessible
Lack of endpoint detection for dumping tool signatures
controls: Credential Guard / LSASS protection
EDR detection for known dumping tool behavior
Least-privilege access to credential stores
ITID-51111.detection: Endpoint detection can flag dumping tool behavior directly; this leaf itself is a triage/rollup point pending confirmation of the specific mechanism.
ITID-51111.response: Treat as a mass-exposure event: identify affected accounts, force resets, and re-classify to the specific ITID-127xx leaf once the technique is confirmed.
metrics: Time to re-triage to specific technical ITID
Number of accounts forced to reset following a dumping event
ITID-51111.notes: This is a lone-child cross-reference stub. Full technical treatment of password-dumping mechanics lives in the ITID-127xx credential-access series and ITID-12133; use this leaf only when the breach-exposure angle, not the technique, is the classification need.

playbook.name: Password Dumping (Data Breach Context)
playbook.description: An attacker has extracted hashed or plaintext credentials from a system (e.g. SAM/NTDS.dit, memory, or a database dump) and those credentials are now exposed to compromise.

steps.title: Detect credential-dumping tool execution or access to credential stores
steps.desc: Review EDR/SIEM alerts for known credential-dumping utilities (e.g. Mimikatz, ProcDump against lsass.exe, secretsdump, registry hive exports of SAM/SECURITY) and for anomalous reads of NTDS.dit or password hash tables.
steps.guidance: Correlate process-execution telemetry with the account that triggered it, and check for LSASS access flagged by EDR. Pivot to authentication logs for the affected account(s) to look for anomalous logons following the dump event.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scope of which credential store was accessed and which accounts' credentials may be exposed.
steps.abort: If no dumping tool or anomalous access is corroborated, downgrade to monitoring and close as a false positive with documented rationale.

steps.title: Identify all accounts whose credentials were present in the dump
steps.desc: Enumerate every account (service, admin, and user) whose password hash or secret was contained in the compromised store or export.
steps.guidance: Use the dump's known scope (single host vs. domain-wide NTDS.dit) to build a full affected-account list; do not assume the attacker only targeted the account used to gain initial access.
steps.outcome: A definitive list of exposed accounts to drive containment actions.

steps.title: Force password reset for all exposed accounts
steps.desc: Immediately expire and force reset of credentials for every account identified as exposed, prioritizing privileged and service accounts.
steps.guidance: Reset in a burst to prevent the attacker from racing the response; coordinate service-account resets with application owners to avoid outages.
steps.outcome: All exposed accounts have new, attacker-unknown credentials.

steps.title: Revoke active sessions and tokens tied to exposed accounts
steps.desc: Invalidate existing Kerberos tickets, SSO sessions, and API tokens for exposed accounts so a reset password cannot be bypassed by an already-established session.
steps.guidance: For domain-wide exposure, consider a krbtgt double-reset in line with established AD-compromise recovery procedures.
steps.outcome: No residual attacker session persists using pre-reset credentials.

steps.title: Remediate the access path used to reach the credential store
steps.desc: Patch or reconfigure the vulnerability, misconfiguration, or excessive privilege that allowed the dumping tool to run or the store to be read.
steps.guidance: Common fixes: enable LSASS protection (Credential Guard/PPL), restrict local admin rights, patch the exploited vulnerability, remove unnecessary domain-admin logon rights on workstations.
steps.outcome: The technique used to obtain the dump can no longer succeed.

steps.title: Enforce MFA on all exposed and privileged accounts
steps.desc: Require multi-factor authentication for exposed accounts going forward so a leaked hash or password alone is insufficient for account takeover.
steps.guidance: Prioritize privileged and remote-access accounts if org-wide MFA rollout is not yet complete.
steps.outcome: Credential exposure alone can no longer result in account compromise.

steps.title: Validate account integrity and restore normal operations
steps.desc: Confirm no unauthorized changes (new admin accounts, mailbox rules, persistence) were made using the dumped credentials before declaring recovery complete.
steps.guidance: Review account audit logs for the period between dump and reset for suspicious modifications.
steps.outcome: Environment confirmed clean and accounts returned to normal operation.

steps.title: Conduct post-incident review of credential storage and access controls
steps.desc: Document root cause, timeline, and remediation, and drive follow-up hardening (LSASS protection baseline, tiered admin model, hash-dumping detection rules).
steps.guidance: Feed detection gaps back into SIEM/EDR use-case tuning.
steps.outcome: Formal report with tracked remediation actions.

ITID-51121.def: A data-breach-context leaf capturing incidents where credentials obtained through phishing were used to access and expose company data, with the classification focus on the breach outcome rather than the phishing delivery method.
ITID-51121.purpose: Provides an intake/cross-reference point for phishing-obtained credentials when the classification need is the resulting data breach, not the phishing campaign mechanics.
scopeIncludes: Breach triage where phished credentials are the confirmed or suspected entry vector
Cases reported as 'account compromised via phishing' where the data-exposure scope is the open question
scopeExcludes: Full phishing campaign analysis and delivery-mechanism detail (see the phishing-specific ITID series under Social Engineering / Initial Access)
Password dumping (ITID-51111)
Credential stuffing (ITID-51131)
ITID-51121.severity: Medium-High, scaling with the sensitivity of data accessible to the compromised account.
ITID-51121.priority: P1 for privileged or data-rich accounts; P2 for standard user accounts pending impact assessment.
ITID-51121.escalation: Escalate to identity security and data owners once account access is confirmed to include sensitive data stores.
indicators: Successful login following a known phishing click
Anomalous access patterns from a recently phished account
Help-desk report of credential entry on a suspicious page
vectors: Credential-harvesting phishing pages
Business email compromise via spoofed login prompts
rootCauses: Insufficient phishing-resistant MFA
User susceptibility absent recent awareness training
controls: Phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/WebAuthn)
Email security gateway with credential-harvesting detection
Conditional access on anomalous sign-in
ITID-51121.detection: Identity provider sign-in risk detections and email security telemetry provide the primary signal; this leaf is a rollup pending confirmation.
ITID-51121.response: Reset the compromised credential, review account access logs for data exposure, and re-classify to the appropriate breach-type leaf based on what was accessed.
metrics: Mean time to detect phished-credential use
Percentage of phishing-derived compromises caught before data access
ITID-51121.notes: This is a lone-child cross-reference stub. Detailed phishing-technique classification lives in the Social Engineering / Initial Access branch of the taxonomy; use this leaf when the concern is the resulting data breach.

playbook.name: Phished Credentials (Data Breach Context)
playbook.description: A user submitted valid credentials to an attacker-controlled phishing page, resulting in the attacker gaining access to accounts or systems.

steps.title: Confirm phishing report and identify the credential-harvesting page
steps.desc: Validate the reported phishing email/site, capture the URL, and determine whether it is an active credential-harvesting kit.
steps.guidance: Use email gateway logs and URL sandboxing to confirm the page harvested credentials rather than just being spam.
steps.outcome: Confirmed phishing vector and harvesting mechanism.
steps.abort: If the reported email did not lead to a working credential-capture page, close as non-incident with documentation.

steps.title: Identify all users who submitted credentials and any resulting anomalous logons
steps.desc: Cross-reference email delivery/click logs against authentication logs to find every user who reached the page and any subsequent suspicious sign-ins (new geography, impossible travel, new device).
steps.guidance: Check SSO/IdP risk-detection signals and mailbox-access logs for post-phish activity such as inbox rule creation or mail forwarding.
steps.outcome: Full list of compromised accounts and any confirmed attacker activity post-compromise.

steps.title: Force password reset and revoke sessions for affected accounts
steps.desc: Reset credentials and terminate all active sessions/refresh tokens for every user who submitted credentials to the phishing page.
steps.guidance: Revoke OAuth app consents and mailbox delegate/forwarding rules created during the compromise window.
steps.outcome: Attacker no longer has valid access via the phished credentials.

steps.title: Block the phishing infrastructure and remove the email from all mailboxes
steps.desc: Block the malicious domain/URL at the email gateway and web proxy, and purge the phishing email from any mailbox that has not yet actioned it.
steps.guidance: Submit the URL for external takedown/blocklisting where appropriate.
steps.outcome: No further users can reach the phishing page from corporate systems.
steps.tool: Email Security Gateway / Secure Web Gateway

steps.title: Enforce phishing-resistant MFA on affected and high-risk accounts
steps.desc: Move affected accounts (and ideally the broader population) to phishing-resistant authentication (FIDO2/WebAuthn) or at minimum enforce MFA to prevent recurrence.
steps.guidance: If push-based MFA was itself the target of fatigue/relay, prioritize number-matching or hardware-key rollout.
steps.outcome: Credential re-phishing alone can no longer result in account takeover.

steps.title: Deploy anti-phishing detection improvements at the email gateway
steps.desc: Tune email security gateway rules and URL/attachment sandboxing to detect and block the specific lure and kit characteristics observed in this campaign.
steps.guidance: Share indicators (sender domains, kit fingerprints) with the email security vendor for signature updates.
steps.outcome: Similar phishing emails are blocked or flagged before reaching users going forward.

steps.title: Validate mailbox and account integrity before returning to normal use
steps.desc: Confirm no persistence (forwarding rules, delegate access, malicious OAuth grants) remains and that account owners can resume normal work.
steps.guidance: Have affected users confirm no unfamiliar activity in their mailbox/account history.
steps.outcome: Accounts confirmed clean and usable.

steps.title: Update phishing awareness training and detection rules
steps.desc: Document the campaign's lure and technique, share indicators org-wide, and target follow-up training/simulated-phishing at the affected population.
steps.guidance: Feed the harvesting domain/kit signature into ongoing detection content.
steps.outcome: Reduced likelihood of repeat success from the same or similar campaign.

ITID-51131.def: A data-breach-context leaf capturing incidents where previously leaked credential pairs were reused against company systems (credential stuffing) and successfully resulted in unauthorized data access.
ITID-51131.purpose: Provides an intake/cross-reference point for credential-stuffing-driven data breaches, distinct from the underlying credential-stuffing attack mechanics.
scopeIncludes: Confirmed account takeover via reused/leaked credential pairs where data exposure is the classification focus
Bulk automated login-attempt campaigns that achieved at least one successful breach
scopeExcludes: Unsuccessful credential-stuffing attempts with no account compromise (an availability/attack-attempt classification elsewhere)
Password dumping that sourced the original credentials (ITID-51111)
ITID-51131.severity: Medium-High, scaling with the number of accounts successfully compromised and data sensitivity.
ITID-51131.priority: P2, escalating to P1 if privileged accounts or bulk customer data are affected.
ITID-51131.escalation: Escalate to identity security when successful logins exceed a small number of accounts or touch sensitive data stores.
indicators: High-volume login attempts from distributed IPs against valid usernames
Successful logins matching known-leaked credential pairs
Spike in failed-then-succeeded login patterns
vectors: Automated credential-stuffing tooling using breached credential lists
Reuse of credentials leaked from unrelated third-party breaches
rootCauses: Lack of MFA enforcement
Absence of rate-limiting/bot mitigation on login endpoints
Users reusing passwords across services
controls: MFA enforcement on all accounts
Bot/rate-limiting protection on authentication endpoints
Breached-password screening at login
ITID-51131.detection: Authentication logs and bot-mitigation telemetry give strong, direct signal for this leaf.
ITID-51131.response: Lock affected accounts, force resets, and review accessed data to determine breach scope and notification obligations.
metrics: Number of accounts compromised per stuffing campaign
Time to detect and block a stuffing campaign
detections: Authentication anomaly and bot-traffic detection rules
ITID-51131.notes: This is a lone-child cross-reference stub focused on the breach outcome of credential stuffing; broader attack-attempt classification (including unsuccessful campaigns) sits elsewhere in the taxonomy.

playbook.name: Credential Stuffing Breach (Data Breach Context)
playbook.description: Automated login attempts using credentials leaked from other breaches successfully authenticated against company accounts, resulting in unauthorized access.

steps.title: Detect credential-stuffing traffic pattern
steps.desc: Identify a spike in failed/successful logins consistent with automated credential-stuffing (high volume, distributed source IPs, non-human timing, known stuffing-tool user agents).
steps.guidance: Correlate with WAF/bot-management logs and login-rate anomalies; distinguish from brute force by the pattern of many distinct usernames each tried a small number of times.
steps.outcome: Confirmed stuffing campaign with a defined attack window.
steps.abort: If the traffic pattern does not match automated stuffing (e.g. isolated failed logins), treat as routine and close.

steps.title: Identify accounts with successful unauthorized logins
steps.desc: Cross-reference the attack window against successful authentications to determine which accounts were actually compromised, not merely targeted.
steps.guidance: Flag successful logins from IPs/user-agents matching the stuffing campaign for further review of post-login activity.
steps.outcome: Definitive list of compromised accounts requiring containment.

steps.title: Force password reset and revoke sessions for compromised accounts
steps.desc: Reset credentials and terminate active sessions for every account with a confirmed unauthorized successful login.
steps.guidance: Prioritize accounts showing post-login activity (data access, profile changes, payment changes).
steps.outcome: Attacker access via stuffed credentials is terminated.

steps.title: Rate-limit and block stuffing traffic at the edge
steps.desc: Apply WAF rate-limiting, IP/ASN blocking, and bot-management challenges to stop the ongoing campaign at the perimeter.
steps.guidance: Use device fingerprinting and CAPTCHA challenges rather than blunt IP blocking where the source pool is large or rotating.
steps.outcome: Stuffing traffic volume drops to negligible levels.

steps.title: Deploy breach-password blocklisting and MFA enforcement
steps.desc: Enforce a check against known-breached password lists at login/password-set time, and require MFA to prevent reuse of leaked credentials from succeeding.
steps.guidance: Consider mandatory password reset for the broader user base if the credential set used originated from a large, unrelated third-party breach.
steps.outcome: Leaked credential reuse can no longer directly result in account takeover.

steps.title: Deploy device fingerprinting and CAPTCHA challenges on login flows
steps.desc: Implement adaptive risk-based challenges (CAPTCHA, device fingerprinting) on authentication endpoints to raise the cost of future automated stuffing attempts.
steps.outcome: Automated stuffing tooling is substantially less effective against the login flow.

steps.title: Verify account integrity and resume normal login volumes
steps.desc: Confirm compromised accounts show no residual unauthorized changes and that legitimate user login success rates have returned to baseline.
steps.guidance: Monitor for a secondary wave of stuffing attempts targeting the same account population.
steps.outcome: Accounts restored and login telemetry back to normal.

steps.title: Review authentication hardening and bot-defense posture
steps.desc: Document the campaign, its source, and effectiveness of defenses, and drive adoption of adaptive rate-limiting, MFA coverage gaps, and breach-list monitoring.
steps.guidance: Consider notifying affected customers if consumer-facing accounts were involved.
steps.outcome: Documented findings with tracked hardening actions.

ITID-51141.def: A data-breach-context leaf capturing incidents where a stolen or hijacked authentication token (session cookie, OAuth token, Kerberos ticket, etc.) was used to access and expose company data.
ITID-51141.purpose: Provides an intake/cross-reference point for session-token or authentication-token theft that resulted in a data breach, distinct from the detailed token-abuse technique series.
scopeIncludes: Breach triage where a stolen token is the confirmed or suspected access vector
Cases where token theft enabled bypass of MFA and led to data exposure
scopeExcludes: Detailed pass-the-hash/pass-the-ticket/token-impersonation technique classification (see the ITID-127xx series, e.g. ITID-12721 through ITID-12749)
Credentials obtained via phishing rather than token theft (ITID-51121)
ITID-51141.severity: High, since token theft frequently bypasses MFA and grants immediate authenticated access.
ITID-51141.priority: P1 whenever token theft is confirmed against a live session with data access.
ITID-51141.escalation: Escalate immediately; revoke sessions/tokens platform-wide for the affected identity and involve identity security.
indicators: Session reuse from an unexpected device/location without a corresponding login event
Token replay detected by conditional access
Anomalous API calls using a valid but unexpectedly-sourced token
vectors: Session cookie theft via malware or adversary-in-the-middle proxy
OAuth token theft/consent phishing
Kerberos ticket theft and reuse
rootCauses: Lack of token binding/session hardening
Long-lived tokens without re-authentication checks
Insufficient monitoring of token issuance and reuse
mitreTechniques: T1550.001 Use Alternate Authentication Material: Application Access Token
controls: Token binding and short token lifetimes
Continuous access evaluation / session revocation on risk signal
Conditional access requiring device compliance
ITID-51141.detection: Identity provider and conditional-access telemetry provide strong signal for anomalous token reuse.
ITID-51141.response: Revoke all active sessions/tokens for the affected identity, force credential and MFA re-registration, and assess data accessed during the token's misuse window.
metrics: Time to revoke compromised tokens
Number of data-breach incidents attributable to token theft
ITID-51141.notes: This is a lone-child cross-reference stub. Full technical treatment of pass-the-hash, pass-the-ticket, and token-impersonation techniques lives in the ITID-127xx series; use this leaf when the breach-exposure outcome is the classification need.

playbook.name: Token Hijacking (Data Breach Context)
playbook.description: An attacker obtained and replayed a valid session, OAuth, or API token to impersonate a legitimate user or service without needing the underlying password.

steps.title: Detect anomalous token use
steps.desc: Identify sign-ins or API calls using a valid token from an unexpected location, device, IP, or with impossible-travel characteristics, or a token used after its expected client context changed.
steps.guidance: Correlate IdP risk signals (token replay, new device without new MFA challenge) with API gateway/access logs for the token's issuer and audience.
steps.outcome: Confirmed hijacked token(s) and the scope of access it granted.
steps.abort: If the anomaly is explained by legitimate user behavior (VPN, travel), close with documentation.

steps.title: Determine how the token was obtained (theft vector)
steps.desc: Investigate the likely acquisition method: token theft via malware/infostealer, cross-site scripting, man-in-the-middle, misconfigured token storage, or leaked in logs/repos.
steps.guidance: Check endpoint telemetry for infostealer indicators and review application logging for accidental token exposure.
steps.outcome: Identified theft vector to inform eradication.

steps.title: Revoke the hijacked token(s) and force re-authentication
steps.desc: Immediately revoke the specific session, OAuth, or API token(s) identified, and invalidate related refresh tokens so the attacker cannot mint new access tokens.
steps.guidance: Revoke at the authorization server / identity provider, not just at the application layer, to ensure refresh-token chains are broken.
steps.outcome: The hijacked token set is no longer valid for any further access.

steps.title: Reset underlying account credentials if theft vector implicates the endpoint or account
steps.desc: Where token theft resulted from account or device compromise (e.g. infostealer malware), reset the user's password in addition to token revocation.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with endpoint remediation if malware is confirmed on the device.
steps.outcome: Both the token and any underlying compromised credential are neutralized.
steps.abort: If theft vector is purely a token-handling flaw (e.g. XSS) with no credential exposure, this step may be skipped.

steps.title: Remediate the token theft vector and harden token lifetimes
steps.desc: Fix the specific weakness that allowed token theft (e.g. patch XSS, enforce HttpOnly/secure cookie flags, remove tokens from logs) and shorten token/session lifetimes with mandatory refresh-token rotation.
steps.guidance: Where the vector was malware, ensure endpoint eradication is tracked as a linked action; where it was an app flaw, engage the owning engineering team.
steps.outcome: The specific theft technique is closed and token exposure windows are reduced going forward.

steps.title: Implement anomalous-token-use detection rules
steps.desc: Deploy or tune detection rules for token replay from unexpected geographies/devices, impossible travel, and token use inconsistent with the issuing session's characteristics.
steps.outcome: Future token hijacking attempts are detected significantly faster.

steps.title: Verify no unauthorized actions were taken with the hijacked token
steps.desc: Review the audit trail of actions performed using the hijacked token during the exposure window and confirm the account/service returns to normal operation.
steps.guidance: Reverse any unauthorized data access or changes discovered.
steps.outcome: Confirmed scope of impact and clean restoration of legitimate access.

steps.title: Review token issuance, storage, and lifetime policies
steps.desc: Document the incident and drive adoption of shorter-lived tokens, refresh-token rotation, and detection rules for anomalous token replay across the environment.
steps.outcome: Documented findings with tracked policy and detection improvements.

ITID-51211.def: An intake classification for incidents in which customer PII (names, addresses, contact details, account identifiers, non-payment/non-health identifiers) has been exposed, accessed without authorization, or exfiltrated, and the exposure mechanism or data category has not yet been, or cannot be, narrowed to a more specific ITID-512xx leaf.
ITID-51211.purpose: Captures a confirmed exposure of customer personally identifiable information that does not cleanly match a more specific PII-exposure or payment-card leaf.
scopeIncludes: Confirmed customer PII exposure of unclear or mixed origin pending further triage
General customer data leaks that are non-health, non-payment-card in nature
Cases spanning multiple exposure vectors where no single specific leaf applies
scopeExcludes: Protected health information breaches (health information breach leaves)
Payment card data breaches (payment card data breach leaves)
Employee-only data exposure (Employee Data Leak leaves)
ITID-51211.severity: Medium-High, scaling with record volume, data sensitivity, and regulatory notification thresholds (e.g., state breach-notification laws).
ITID-51211.priority: P2 by default; escalate to P1 if record count is large, data includes sensitive identifiers (SSN, government ID), or public/media exposure is confirmed.
ITID-51211.escalation: Escalate to privacy/legal counsel and data protection officer as soon as customer PII exposure is confirmed, in parallel with SOC containment.
indicators: Customer records found in a public location or paste site
Customer complaints of unsolicited contact referencing account details
Unusual bulk export or query activity against a customer data store
vectors: Misconfigured access controls on customer data stores
Compromised credentials used to query customer databases
Third-party integration errors exposing customer records
rootCauses: Insufficient access control review on customer-data systems
Lack of data classification and handling standards
Absence of monitoring on bulk data access
controls: Data loss prevention (DLP) on customer data repositories
Least-privilege access control on customer databases
Egress monitoring for bulk data transfers
ITID-51211.detection: Detection depends on DLP and database activity monitoring; unclassified leaks are frequently first identified externally (customer report, media, dark web) rather than internally.
ITID-51211.response: Triage to confirm scope and data categories, then reclassify to a more specific leaf where possible; initiate privacy/legal breach assessment regardless.
metrics: Number of unclassified customer data leak incidents pending reclassification
Time to reclassify into a specific leaf
Records exposed per incident
detections: DLP alerts on customer data repositories
ITID-51211.notes: This is an intake/catch-all leaf; incidents should be reclassified into a more specific customer-data leaf as soon as the exposure mechanism and data category are confirmed.

playbook.name: Customer Data Leak (PII Exposure Context)
playbook.description: Customer personally identifiable information was exposed to unauthorized parties through a breach, misconfiguration, or unauthorized disclosure.

steps.title: Confirm the exposure and identify the affected data store
steps.desc: Validate the report or alert (e.g. exposed database, misconfigured bucket, third-party notification) and identify exactly which system holds the exposed customer PII.
steps.guidance: Use DLP alerts, cloud security posture findings, or the reporting party's evidence to pinpoint the source.
steps.outcome: Confirmed exposed data store and access method.
steps.abort: If the report cannot be corroborated against any real exposure, document and close as unsubstantiated.

steps.title: Determine scope: records, data fields, and customers affected
steps.desc: Quantify how many customer records were exposed and which specific PII fields (name, address, SSN, financial data, etc.) were included, and the exposure time window.
steps.guidance: This scoping directly drives regulatory notification thresholds and content, so be precise and conservative when uncertain.
steps.outcome: A defined, defensible scope statement of affected customers and data elements.

steps.title: Cut off the exposure vector
steps.desc: Close public access, revoke the unauthorized credential/link, or take the misconfigured resource offline to stop further exposure.
steps.guidance: Preserve logs and a snapshot of the exposed configuration before remediating, for forensic and regulatory purposes.
steps.outcome: No further unauthorized access to customer PII is possible via this vector.

steps.title: Escalate to Legal/Compliance/Privacy for breach-notification assessment
steps.desc: Engage Legal, Compliance, and the Privacy office immediately to assess regulatory notification obligations (state breach-notification laws, GDPR/CCPA as applicable) and establish the notification timeline.
steps.guidance: Do not wait for full forensic completion to begin this engagement — most breach-notification laws start clocks from discovery, not full scoping.
steps.outcome: Legal/Compliance has opened a formal breach assessment with a tracked notification deadline.

steps.title: Remediate the root-cause vulnerability or misconfiguration
steps.desc: Fix the underlying flaw (misconfigured access control, unpatched vulnerability, insecure API) that allowed the exposure.
steps.guidance: Conduct a broader sweep for the same misconfiguration pattern elsewhere in the environment.
steps.outcome: The exposure vector cannot recur via the same root cause.

steps.title: Audit for the same misconfiguration pattern across other customer-data systems
steps.desc: Proactively scan other systems and repositories for the same class of access-control misconfiguration that caused this exposure.
steps.outcome: No other systems carry the same exposure risk.

steps.title: Execute customer and regulatory notifications and support workflows
steps.desc: Send required notifications to affected customers and regulators per the Legal/Compliance-determined timeline, and stand up support (credit monitoring, call center) as applicable.
steps.guidance: Coordinate messaging with Communications/PR to ensure consistency.
steps.outcome: Notification obligations met within required timeframes.

steps.title: Conduct post-incident review of data protection controls
steps.desc: Document root cause, timeline, and remediation, and drive follow-up (access reviews, DLP tuning, cloud posture guardrails) to prevent recurrence.
steps.outcome: Formal report with tracked remediation actions.

ITID-51221.def: An intake classification for incidents in which employee PII (HR records, payroll data, benefits information, home addresses, national ID numbers) has been exposed, accessed without authorization, or exfiltrated, and the exposure mechanism has not been, or cannot be, narrowed further.
ITID-51221.purpose: Captures a confirmed exposure of employee personally identifiable information that does not cleanly match a more specific leaf.
scopeIncludes: Confirmed employee PII exposure of unclear or mixed origin pending triage
HR/payroll/benefits data leaks not tied to a specific sub-category
Exposure affecting current or former employees
scopeExcludes: Customer PII exposure (Customer Data Leak leaves)
Protected health information tied to employee benefits claims (Health Information Breach leaves)
Payment card data exposure
ITID-51221.severity: Medium-High, scaling with the number of employees affected and sensitivity of the data (e.g., SSNs, bank account numbers for payroll).
ITID-51221.priority: P2 by default; escalate to P1 if the data includes government identifiers or financial account details enabling identity theft.
ITID-51221.escalation: Escalate to HR, legal/privacy, and the data protection officer immediately; employee data breaches carry distinct internal-relations and works-council/union notification obligations in many jurisdictions.
indicators: HR or payroll system export activity outside normal cycles
Employee reports of phishing referencing internal HR details
Employee records found exposed externally
vectors: Compromised HR/payroll system credentials
Misconfigured file shares containing HR exports
Phishing targeting HR/payroll staff
rootCauses: Overly broad access to HR/payroll systems
Lack of encryption on HR data exports
Insufficient monitoring of HR system access
controls: Access control review on HR/payroll systems
DLP on HR data exports
Encryption of HR data at rest and in transit
ITID-51221.detection: HR/payroll systems typically have weaker monitoring than production systems, so detection often relies on manual review or external notification.
ITID-51221.response: Confirm scope with HR, reclassify where possible, and initiate employee notification per applicable law and policy.
metrics: Number of unclassified employee data leak incidents
Employees affected per incident
Time to HR/legal notification
ITID-51221.notes: This is an intake/catch-all leaf; incidents should be reclassified once the exposure mechanism and affected data categories are confirmed.

playbook.name: Employee Data Leak (PII Exposure Context)
playbook.description: Employee personally identifiable information (e.g. HR records, payroll data, SSNs) was exposed to unauthorized parties through a breach, misconfiguration, or unauthorized disclosure.

steps.title: Confirm the exposure and identify the affected HR/payroll system
steps.desc: Validate the report or alert and identify exactly which system (HRIS, payroll platform, benefits portal, shared drive) holds the exposed employee PII.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with HR IT and the HRIS/payroll vendor if the exposed system is third-party hosted.
steps.outcome: Confirmed exposed system and access method.
steps.abort: If the report cannot be corroborated, document and close as unsubstantiated.

steps.title: Determine scope: employees and data fields affected
steps.desc: Quantify how many employees and which specific fields (SSN, bank details, salary, health/benefits data) were exposed and over what time window.
steps.guidance: Flag any exposure of SSNs or bank details as high-severity given identity-theft risk.
steps.outcome: A defined scope statement of affected employees and data elements.

steps.title: Cut off the exposure vector
steps.desc: Revoke unauthorized access, disable the exposed share/link, or take the affected system offline to stop further exposure.
steps.guidance: Preserve access logs and a snapshot of the misconfiguration before remediating.
steps.outcome: No further unauthorized access to employee PII is possible via this vector.

steps.title: Escalate to Legal/Compliance/HR/Privacy for breach-notification assessment
steps.desc: Engage Legal, Compliance, HR leadership, and the Privacy office to assess state breach-notification obligations and establish the employee-notification timeline.
steps.guidance: HR must be looped in given the employment-relationship sensitivity and potential union/labor-relations implications.
steps.outcome: A tracked breach assessment with a defined notification deadline and HR-approved communications.

steps.title: Remediate the root-cause vulnerability or misconfiguration
steps.desc: Fix the underlying flaw (access-control misconfiguration, unpatched vendor system, overly broad sharing permissions) that allowed the exposure.
steps.guidance: Review other HR-adjacent systems for the same class of misconfiguration.
steps.outcome: The exposure vector cannot recur via the same root cause.

steps.title: Audit for the same misconfiguration pattern across other HR-adjacent systems
steps.desc: Proactively scan other HR, payroll, and benefits systems for the same class of access-control or sharing misconfiguration.
steps.outcome: No other HR-adjacent systems carry the same exposure risk.

steps.title: Execute employee and regulatory notifications and support offerings
steps.desc: Notify affected employees and regulators per the determined timeline, and offer identity-theft protection/credit monitoring where SSNs or financial data were exposed.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with HR on internal communications to manage employee trust and morale impact.
steps.outcome: Notification and support obligations met within required timeframes.

steps.title: Conduct post-incident review of HR data protection controls
steps.desc: Document root cause and remediation, and drive follow-up (access reviews, vendor security assessment, DLP tuning on HR systems) to prevent recurrence.
steps.outcome: Formal report with tracked remediation actions.

ITID-51231.def: An incident in which an unauthorized party (external attacker, unauthorized internal user, or insider exceeding authorized scope) accesses, views, or exfiltrates protected health information (PHI) held in an EHR or clinical information system.
ITID-51231.purpose: Captures unauthorized access to an Electronic Health Records (EHR) system as a distinct, high-regulatory-stakes PHI exposure pathway.
scopeIncludes: External compromise of EHR system credentials or infrastructure
Internal user accessing PHI outside their treatment/payment/operations authorization ('snooping')
Bulk export or query of patient records from an EHR platform
scopeExcludes: PHI exposed via misdirected fax, email, or mail (Misdirected Medical Communication leaf)
PHI on a lost or stolen portable device (Lost/Stolen Portable Medical Device leaf)
PHI breach originating at a third-party business associate (Third-Party Healthcare Vendor leaf)
ITID-51231.severity: High, given HIPAA/HITECH (or equivalent regional health-privacy law) breach notification thresholds and reputational sensitivity of clinical data.
ITID-51231.priority: P1 for any confirmed unauthorized EHR access affecting patient records; P2 for suspected but unconfirmed access pending audit log review.
ITID-51231.escalation: Escalate immediately to the privacy/compliance officer (HIPAA Privacy/Security Officer) and legal; breach risk assessment and regulator notification clocks may start at time of discovery.
indicators: EHR audit log showing access outside a user's assigned patient panel or department
Break-glass/emergency access usage without a corresponding clinical justification
Anomalous bulk record retrieval from the EHR
vectors: Compromised clinician or staff EHR credentials
Insider snooping using legitimate but unauthorized access
Exploitation of EHR application vulnerabilities
rootCauses: Insufficient role-based access control granularity in the EHR
Lack of proactive audit log review for anomalous access patterns
Weak authentication on clinical system accounts
mitreTechniques: T1213.003 Data from Information Repositories: Code Repositories
controls: EHR audit log monitoring and behavioral analytics
Role-based access control aligned to minimum necessary standard
Break-glass access review process
ITID-51231.detection: EHR audit logging is generally strong and purpose-built for this scenario; the primary gap is proactive review rather than log availability.
ITID-51231.response: Pull and review EHR audit trails immediately, determine scope of patient records affected, and engage privacy/compliance for breach risk assessment.
metrics: Number of confirmed unauthorized EHR access events per period
Patient records affected per incident
Time from access to detection
ITID-51231.notes: Note: mapped MITRE technique T1213.003 as listed in the ATT&CK Enterprise matrix is 'Data from Information Repositories: Code Repositories'; the closest applicable sub-technique conceptually for clinical repositories is data-from-information-repositories generally. Retained per instruction for medical records collection.

playbook.name: Unauthorized Access to Electronic Health Records (EHR) System
playbook.description: An unauthorized party accessed the organization's EHR system, exposing protected health information (PHI) subject to HIPAA.

steps.title: Confirm unauthorized EHR access and identify accessed records
steps.desc: Review EHR audit logs to confirm the unauthorized access event, identifying the accessing account, method, and which patient records were viewed, exported, or modified.
steps.guidance: EHR systems typically maintain detailed access audit trails required for HIPAA compliance — use these as the primary evidence source.
steps.outcome: Confirmed unauthorized access with a defined list of accessed patient records.
steps.abort: If the access is confirmed as authorized/legitimate upon review, close as a non-incident with documentation.

steps.title: Determine the access method and scope of PHI exposure
steps.desc: Establish whether access came via compromised credentials, an exploited vulnerability, or misuse of legitimate access, and quantify the number of patients and PHI data elements exposed.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with the HIPAA Security/Privacy Officer early since this scoping determines breach-notification thresholds under HIPAA.
steps.outcome: A defined scope statement suitable for HIPAA breach-risk assessment.

steps.title: Revoke unauthorized access and reset compromised credentials
steps.desc: Immediately disable the unauthorized account/session and reset any compromised credentials used to gain EHR access.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with clinical IT to avoid disrupting legitimate patient-care access during containment.
steps.outcome: Unauthorized access to the EHR system is terminated.

steps.title: Escalate to HIPAA Privacy/Security Officer and Legal for breach-risk assessment
steps.desc: Engage the designated HIPAA Privacy and Security Officer and Legal/Compliance to perform the required four-factor breach-risk assessment and determine notification obligations to individuals, HHS, and potentially media.
steps.guidance: HIPAA's 60-day notification clock begins at discovery — initiate this assessment in parallel with technical containment, not after.
steps.outcome: A documented HIPAA breach-risk assessment with a tracked notification timeline.

steps.title: Remediate the vulnerability or access-control gap in the EHR system
steps.desc: Fix the exploited vulnerability, tighten role-based access controls, or address the credential-compromise root cause within the EHR system and its supporting infrastructure.
steps.guidance: Review EHR role/permission assignments for excessive access as part of remediation.
steps.outcome: The access path exploited cannot be reused.

steps.title: Review EHR role-based access assignments for excessive privilege
steps.desc: Conduct a role/permission audit across the EHR user base to identify and remove excessive access grants that go beyond clinical need-to-know.
steps.outcome: EHR access is aligned to least-privilege, reducing the pool of accounts that could enable similar unauthorized access.

steps.title: Execute HIPAA-required notifications and restore normal clinical operations
steps.desc: Notify affected individuals, HHS, and media (if threshold met) per HIPAA Breach Notification Rule timelines, and confirm EHR system integrity before resuming full clinical use.
steps.guidance: Coordinate notification content and timing with Legal and Communications.
steps.outcome: Notification obligations met and EHR system confirmed safe for clinical use.

steps.title: Conduct post-incident HIPAA compliance review
steps.desc: Document root cause, response timeline, and remediation, and drive follow-up (access audits, EHR logging/alerting improvements) reported to the compliance committee.
steps.outcome: Formal report with tracked remediation actions and compliance sign-off.

ITID-51232.def: An incident in which protected health information is disclosed to an unintended recipient via fax, email, physical mail, or similar communication channel due to misaddressing, mis-attachment, or process error.
ITID-51232.purpose: Captures PHI breaches caused by human error in routing medical communications, distinct from system-level unauthorized access.
scopeIncludes: PHI faxed or emailed to the wrong recipient
Physical mail containing PHI sent to the wrong address or with visible PHI through an envelope window
Bulk mail/email merge errors exposing PHI across multiple unintended recipients
scopeExcludes: Unauthorized system-level access to the EHR (EHR Unauthorized Access leaf)
Loss or theft of a portable device containing PHI (Lost/Stolen Portable Medical Device leaf)
Business-associate-caused misdirection occurring entirely within a vendor's environment (Third-Party Healthcare Vendor leaf)
ITID-51232.severity: Medium, scaling with the volume of records misdirected and whether the recipient is known/trusted versus unknown.
ITID-51232.priority: P2 by default; escalate to P1 for bulk misdirection events affecting many patients simultaneously.
ITID-51232.escalation: Escalate to the privacy officer for a breach risk assessment; attempt recall/retrieval from the recipient as an immediate mitigating action.
indicators: Recipient or intended patient reports receiving/not receiving medical correspondence
Returned mail or bounced email flagged as containing PHI
Fax transmission log showing an incorrect destination number
vectors: Manual data entry error in recipient fax number, email address, or mailing address
Mail-merge or template error in bulk correspondence
Autocomplete selecting the wrong contact in email clients
rootCauses: Lack of recipient verification step before sending PHI
Absence of encrypted, access-controlled channels for routine medical correspondence
Insufficient staff training on PHI handling procedures
controls: Recipient verification/double-check procedures for PHI correspondence
Encrypted email/secure patient portal in place of unencrypted fax or email
Fax number/address validation against a maintained directory
ITID-51232.detection: Little to no technical detection surface; this category is almost entirely process-error driven and detected via recipient reports or manual audit, not security tooling.
ITID-51232.response: Attempt immediate recall of the misdirected communication, document the error, and route to the privacy officer for breach risk assessment and notification determination.
metrics: Number of misdirected PHI communications per period
Percentage successfully recalled/retrieved
Records affected per incident
ITID-51232.notes: No ATT&CK Enterprise mapping applies; this is a human-error/process-failure incident type rather than an adversary technique, so tactics and techniques are intentionally left empty.

playbook.name: PHI Breach via Misdirected Medical Communication (Fax/Email/Mail)
playbook.description: Protected health information was sent to the wrong recipient via fax, email, or physical mail, resulting in unauthorized disclosure.

steps.title: Confirm the misdirected communication and identify recipient and content
steps.desc: Validate the report (from sender, recipient, or monitoring) and determine exactly what PHI was sent, via which channel, and to whom.
steps.guidance: Obtain a copy or description of the actual content sent, not just the fact that a misdirection occurred.
steps.outcome: Confirmed content, channel, and unintended recipient.
steps.abort: If the recipient is confirmed to be authorized (e.g. correct provider, misfiled but not misdirected), close as non-incident.
steps.tool: Fax logs / Email logs / Mail tracking

steps.title: Determine number of patients and data elements affected
steps.desc: Quantify whether this was a single-patient or batch disclosure and which PHI fields were included.
steps.guidance: Check whether the same misdirection pattern (e.g. a stale fax number, outdated distribution list) affected other transmissions.
steps.outcome: A defined scope for HIPAA breach-risk assessment.

steps.title: Contact the unintended recipient to request destruction/return and confirm no further disclosure
steps.desc: Reach out to the recipient promptly to request they destroy or return the material and confirm it was not further shared, viewed, or copied.
steps.guidance: Document the recipient's response in writing where possible, as this affects the HIPAA breach-risk assessment (mitigating factor).
steps.outcome: Confirmation of destruction/return or, at minimum, documented mitigation efforts.
steps.abort: If the recipient cannot be reached or refuses, document this for the risk assessment and notification decision.

steps.title: Escalate to HIPAA Privacy Officer for breach-risk assessment
steps.desc: Engage the Privacy Officer to conduct the four-factor HIPAA breach-risk assessment, factoring in the mitigation obtained from the recipient.
steps.outcome: A documented risk assessment determining whether formal notification is required.

steps.title: Correct the underlying error causing misdirection
steps.desc: Update the incorrect fax number, email address, or mailing distribution list, and verify no other stale entries exist in the same source list.
steps.guidance: Implement a pre-send verification step (e.g. confirmation screen, cover-sheet double-check) for high-volume PHI transmission channels.
steps.outcome: The specific addressing error cannot recur.

steps.title: Audit distribution lists and fax/email directories for other stale entries
steps.desc: Review other frequently used PHI-transmission distribution lists and directories for similar outdated or incorrect entries beyond the one that caused this incident.
steps.outcome: Other latent misdirection risks in transmission lists are identified and corrected proactively.

steps.title: Notify affected patient(s) if required and close out the assessment
steps.desc: Complete required patient notification per the Privacy Officer's determination and close the incident record.
steps.outcome: Notification obligations (if any) fulfilled and incident formally closed.

steps.title: Review transmission verification controls for PHI communications
steps.desc: Document the incident and drive process improvements (address-list hygiene, verification prompts, staff retraining) to reduce future misdirection.
steps.outcome: Documented findings with tracked process improvements.

ITID-51233.def: An incident in which a laptop, tablet, smartphone, USB drive, or other portable medical device or storage medium containing protected health information is lost or stolen.
ITID-51233.purpose: Captures PHI breaches arising from the physical loss or theft of a portable device, a persistently common healthcare breach vector.
scopeIncludes: Lost or stolen unencrypted laptop containing patient data
Stolen mobile device with clinical app access or cached PHI
Misplaced portable storage media (USB drives, external hard drives) containing patient records
scopeExcludes: Remote/network-based unauthorized EHR access (EHR Unauthorized Access leaf)
PHI misdirected via fax/email/mail (Misdirected Medical Communication leaf)
Device loss at a third-party business associate's facility (Third-Party Healthcare Vendor leaf)
ITID-51233.severity: High if the device was unencrypted or lacked remote-wipe capability; Medium-Low if full-disk encryption and remote wipe are confirmed and no PHI was locally cached.
ITID-51233.priority: P1 pending confirmation of encryption status; downgrade to P3 once encryption is verified and no compromise indicators exist.
ITID-51233.escalation: Escalate to the privacy officer immediately; encryption status determines whether the loss constitutes a reportable breach under most health-privacy regimes.
indicators: Employee report of a lost or stolen device
Mobile device management (MDM) system reporting a device as offline/unreachable for wipe
Physical security report of theft from a vehicle, facility, or residence
vectors: Opportunistic theft of an unattended device
Device left in an unsecured location (vehicle, public transit)
Lack of remote lock/wipe enrollment allowing continued data access after loss
rootCauses: Devices not enrolled in full-disk encryption or MDM
Lack of policy restricting local caching of PHI on portable devices
Insufficient physical security awareness training for staff carrying PHI-bearing devices
controls: Mandatory full-disk encryption on all portable devices handling PHI
MDM enrollment with remote lock/wipe capability
Policy restricting local PHI storage in favor of thin-client/VDI access
ITID-51233.detection: Detection relies on employee self-reporting and MDM check-in status rather than active technical monitoring; there is limited signal until the device is reported missing.
ITID-51233.response: Immediately attempt remote lock/wipe via MDM, confirm encryption status, and route to the privacy officer for breach risk assessment.
metrics: Number of lost/stolen device incidents per period
Percentage of affected devices with confirmed encryption
Time from loss to remote wipe attempt
ITID-51233.notes: No ATT&CK Enterprise mapping applies; physical device loss/theft is outside the scope of ATT&CK Enterprise's network-intrusion technique set.

playbook.name: PHI Breach via Lost/Stolen Portable Medical Device
playbook.description: A portable device containing protected health information (e.g. laptop, tablet, mobile phone, USB drive) was lost or stolen, resulting in potential unauthorized disclosure.

steps.title: Confirm the loss/theft and identify the device's data content and encryption status
steps.desc: Validate the report and determine what PHI was stored on the device, and critically, whether the device and its storage were encrypted.
steps.guidance: Check MDM/asset-management records for the device's encryption status and last-known content sync — encryption status is the key factor in HIPAA breach-risk assessment (a properly encrypted device loss is generally not a reportable breach).
steps.outcome: Confirmed device content and encryption status.
steps.abort: If the device is recovered intact with no evidence of access, close as non-incident with documentation.

steps.title: Determine number of patients and data elements potentially exposed
steps.desc: If unencrypted or encryption status cannot be confirmed, quantify the scope of PHI that was or could have been stored on the device.
steps.guidance: Use backup/sync logs to reconstruct the device's likely data content at time of loss.
steps.outcome: A defined scope for HIPAA breach-risk assessment.

steps.title: Remote-wipe the device and revoke its access credentials
steps.desc: Trigger a remote wipe via MDM if the device is enrolled, and revoke any credentials, certificates, or tokens stored on or used to access data from the device.
steps.guidance: Attempt wipe confirmation; if the device is offline, flag for wipe-on-next-connect and revoke access at the account level regardless.
steps.outcome: Device access to corporate/PHI systems is terminated and locally stored data is rendered inaccessible where possible.

steps.title: Escalate to HIPAA Privacy Officer for breach-risk assessment
steps.desc: Engage the Privacy Officer to conduct the breach-risk assessment based on encryption status and scope, determining notification obligations.
steps.guidance: An encrypted-device loss meeting HIPAA's safe-harbor standard may not require notification — document this determination clearly either way.
steps.outcome: A documented risk assessment and notification determination.

steps.title: Close the gap enabling unencrypted PHI on portable devices
steps.desc: If the device was not properly encrypted per policy, remediate the enrollment/encryption gap and audit other devices for the same deficiency.
steps.guidance: Review MDM enforcement policy to ensure encryption is mandatory and verified before a device can sync PHI.
steps.outcome: No other portable devices in the fleet carry the same exposure.

steps.title: Audit device fleet for encryption and MDM enrollment compliance
steps.desc: Run a fleet-wide compliance check to confirm all portable devices with PHI access are properly enrolled in MDM and encrypted per policy.
steps.outcome: Full visibility into fleet-wide compliance with encryption policy, closing any additional latent exposure.

steps.title: Notify affected patients if required and reissue device
steps.desc: Complete required notifications per the Privacy Officer's determination and provide the employee a replacement, compliant device.
steps.outcome: Notification obligations (if any) met and normal operations restored for the employee.

steps.title: Review mobile device management and encryption enforcement policy
steps.desc: Document the incident and drive fleet-wide encryption verification and physical-security awareness training for staff carrying PHI on portable devices.
steps.outcome: Documented findings with tracked policy improvements.

ITID-51234.def: An incident in which a third-party business associate, healthcare technology vendor, billing/claims processor, or other contracted party experiences a breach that exposes PHI the organization is responsible for as a covered entity.
ITID-51234.purpose: Captures PHI breaches originating at a third-party healthcare vendor or business associate, where the organization's own controls are not the point of failure.
scopeIncludes: Breach at a claims clearinghouse, billing vendor, or medical transcription service
Breach at a cloud EHR/practice-management SaaS provider
Business associate subcontractor breach flowing up through the associate agreement
scopeExcludes: Breach occurring directly within the organization's own EHR (EHR Unauthorized Access leaf)
Internal misdirected communication (Misdirected Medical Communication leaf)
Non-healthcare vendor breaches of operational data (Vendor Data Breach leaf under Supply Chain Data Breach)
ITID-51234.severity: High; the organization retains regulatory notification responsibility as the covered entity even though the failure originated with the associate.
ITID-51234.priority: P1 upon notification from the business associate; treat as an active incident until scope and affected patient count are confirmed.
ITID-51234.escalation: Escalate to privacy/compliance and legal immediately upon business associate notification; review the business associate agreement (BAA) for contractual notification and liability terms.
indicators: Formal breach notification received from a business associate under BAA terms
Media or regulatory disclosure naming a vendor used by the organization
Unusual claims or billing activity traced to a vendor-side compromise
vectors: Compromise of the vendor's own systems (ransomware, credential theft, misconfiguration)
Vendor subcontractor breach not disclosed until downstream
Vendor insider misuse of PHI in its care
rootCauses: Insufficient vendor security due diligence prior to onboarding
BAA lacking specific security control or notification-timeliness requirements
Lack of ongoing vendor risk monitoring
controls: Business associate agreement (BAA) with defined security and notification terms
Periodic vendor security risk assessments
Contractual right-to-audit clauses for critical healthcare vendors
ITID-51234.detection: Minimal direct technical detection; the organization typically learns of the breach through vendor notification rather than its own monitoring.
ITID-51234.response: Confirm scope of affected patients with the vendor, assess BAA obligations, and coordinate joint or organization-led breach notification as required.
metrics: Number of business-associate-originated PHI breaches per period
Time from vendor notification to patient notification
Vendors with overdue security assessments
ITID-51234.notes: Cross-reference the Supply Chain Data Breach category (Vendor Data Breach leaves) for the general non-healthcare vendor-breach pattern this leaf specializes for PHI.

playbook.name: Third-Party Healthcare Vendor/Business Associate PHI Breach
playbook.description: A HIPAA business associate or third-party healthcare vendor experienced a breach exposing PHI the organization entrusted to them.

steps.title: Receive and validate the business associate's breach notification
steps.desc: Formally receive the business associate's (BA) breach notification and validate the reported facts against the Business Associate Agreement (BAA) obligations.
steps.guidance: Confirm the BA notified within the timeframe required by the BAA; request their forensic findings and evidence.
steps.outcome: Confirmed understanding of what the BA reported and any gaps in their disclosure.
steps.abort: If the BA's report does not actually involve the organization's PHI, document and close.

steps.title: Independently assess scope of the organization's PHI involved
steps.desc: Determine which of the organization's patients and PHI data elements were within the BA's affected systems, rather than relying solely on the BA's characterization.
steps.guidance: Request detailed record-level information from the BA; do not accept a vague scope statement given notification-timeline dependencies.
steps.outcome: An independently verified scope of impact to the organization's patients.

steps.title: Require the BA to contain the breach and suspend further data transfer if warranted
steps.desc: Direct the BA, per BAA terms, to contain their breach and, if their environment remains compromised, suspend further data feeds/access to that system until contained.
steps.guidance: Escalate through the vendor management/procurement relationship if the BA is unresponsive.
steps.outcome: No further exposure of the organization's PHI through the BA's compromised environment.

steps.title: Escalate to Legal/Compliance and HIPAA Privacy Officer for notification-obligation determination
steps.desc: Engage Legal, Compliance, and the Privacy Officer to determine the organization's own notification obligations to individuals and HHS, which are not waived by the BA's separate notification.
steps.guidance: As the covered entity, the organization typically retains ultimate notification responsibility to patients even when a BA caused the breach.
steps.outcome: A documented determination of the organization's notification obligations and timeline.

steps.title: Verify BA remediation and reassess the BAA/vendor risk posture
steps.desc: Confirm the BA has remediated the root cause, and reassess whether the BAA's security requirements and the vendor's risk rating need revision.
steps.guidance: Consider requiring a third-party security assessment of the BA before resuming full data sharing.
steps.outcome: Confirmed BA remediation and updated vendor risk documentation.

steps.title: Review all other business associates against the same risk pattern
steps.desc: Assess other BAs handling comparable PHI for the same security control gap that caused this breach, using vendor risk assessment records.
steps.outcome: Other BA relationships are reviewed and remediated where the same risk pattern exists.

steps.title: Execute patient and regulatory notifications
steps.desc: Send required notifications to affected patients and HHS per the determined timeline, coordinating messaging with the BA where appropriate.
steps.outcome: Notification obligations met within required timeframes.

steps.title: Review business associate security requirements and oversight process
steps.desc: Document the incident and drive improvements to BAA security clauses, vendor risk assessment cadence, and ongoing BA monitoring.
steps.outcome: Documented findings with tracked vendor-oversight improvements.

ITID-51235.def: An intake classification for incidents involving exposure of protected health information where the exposure mechanism (system access, misdirected communication, device loss, or vendor breach) has not yet been, or cannot be, determined.
ITID-51235.purpose: Captures a confirmed PHI/health information breach that does not cleanly match a more specific leaf under Health Information Breach.
scopeIncludes: Confirmed PHI exposure of unclear or mixed origin pending triage
Health information leaks spanning multiple exposure vectors
scopeExcludes: Unauthorized EHR access with a confirmed system-access vector (EHR Unauthorized Access leaf)
Misdirected medical communication with a confirmed process-error vector (Misdirected Medical Communication leaf)
Confirmed device loss/theft (Lost/Stolen Portable Medical Device leaf)
Confirmed business associate origin (Third-Party Healthcare Vendor leaf)
ITID-51235.severity: High by default given the sensitivity of health data, pending reclassification and refined severity assessment.
ITID-51235.priority: P1 pending triage; reclassify to a specific leaf and reassess priority as soon as the exposure mechanism is confirmed.
ITID-51235.escalation: Escalate to the privacy officer immediately; do not wait for reclassification before beginning the breach risk assessment clock.
indicators: Report of a possible PHI exposure with insufficient detail to determine mechanism
Third-party report (patient, researcher, media) of exposed health data of unclear origin
vectors: Unknown pending investigation
rootCauses: Unknown pending investigation
controls: Standard PHI breach intake and triage process
ITID-51235.detection: Varies entirely by eventual root cause; this leaf exists to hold incidents during the triage window.
ITID-51235.response: Rapidly triage to determine exposure mechanism and reclassify; begin privacy/legal breach assessment in parallel regardless of classification status.
metrics: Number of unclassified health information breach incidents pending reclassification
Time to reclassification
ITID-51235.notes: This is an intake/catch-all leaf; incidents should be reclassified into a specific Health Information Breach leaf as soon as the exposure mechanism is confirmed.

playbook.name: Unclassified / General Health Information Breach
playbook.description: Protected health information was exposed or accessed without authorization through a mechanism not otherwise classified, requiring HIPAA-driven investigation and response.

steps.title: Confirm the reported PHI exposure and identify the affected system or process
steps.desc: Validate the initial report and identify the system, process, or event through which PHI was exposed or accessed without authorization.
steps.guidance: Interview the reporting party and pull relevant access/audit logs for the suspected system before assuming a specific vector.
steps.outcome: Confirmed exposure with an identified source system or process.
steps.abort: If the report cannot be substantiated, document and close as unsubstantiated.

steps.title: Scope affected patients and PHI data elements
steps.desc: Determine the number of patients and which PHI fields were involved, and establish the exposure time window.
steps.guidance: Coordinate with the HIPAA Privacy/Security Officer early to align scoping with breach-risk-assessment requirements.
steps.outcome: A defined scope statement suitable for HIPAA breach-risk assessment.

steps.title: Stop the ongoing exposure
steps.desc: Take whatever action is necessary to halt further unauthorized access or disclosure — revoking access, disabling a feature, or isolating a system, based on the identified vector.
steps.outcome: No further unauthorized exposure of PHI is occurring.

steps.title: Escalate to HIPAA Privacy/Security Officer and Legal for breach-risk assessment
steps.desc: Engage the Privacy/Security Officer and Legal/Compliance to conduct the four-factor HIPAA breach-risk assessment and determine notification obligations.
steps.guidance: Initiate in parallel with containment given the 60-day notification clock from discovery.
steps.outcome: A documented breach-risk assessment with a tracked notification timeline.

steps.title: Remediate the root cause enabling the exposure
steps.desc: Fix the underlying vulnerability, misconfiguration, or process gap identified during investigation.
steps.outcome: The identified root cause can no longer result in PHI exposure.

steps.title: Sweep for related exposure across similar systems or processes
steps.desc: Proactively check other systems or processes sharing the same root-cause characteristic for similar exposure risk.
steps.outcome: No other systems/processes carry the same exposure risk.

steps.title: Execute required notifications and confirm normal operations
steps.desc: Notify affected individuals, HHS, and media as required per the risk assessment, and confirm the affected system/process has returned to secure operation.
steps.outcome: Notification obligations met and operations confirmed secure.

steps.title: Conduct post-incident HIPAA compliance review
steps.desc: Document root cause, response timeline, and remediation for the compliance committee, and drive follow-up controls.
steps.outcome: Formal report with tracked remediation actions.

ITID-51241.def: An incident in which malware installed on point-of-sale (POS) terminals or the POS network captures payment card data (track data, PAN, CVV) from card-present transactions as they are processed.
ITID-51241.purpose: Captures payment card data theft via malware implanted on point-of-sale terminals or systems, a classic and highly regulated retail breach pattern.
scopeIncludes: RAM-scraping malware capturing unencrypted card data in POS terminal memory
Malware harvesting card data via a compromised POS network segment
Persistent POS malware exfiltrating batches of card data over time
scopeExcludes: Card-not-present skimming on an e-commerce checkout page (E-Commerce Payment Page Skimmer leaf)
Physical skimming hardware attached to a card reader (Physical Card Skimming Device Breach leaf)
Breach occurring at the payment processor/gateway rather than the merchant's own POS (Compromised Payment Processor leaf)
ITID-51241.severity: High; POS malware breaches typically affect large volumes of card-present transactions and trigger PCI DSS forensic investigation (PFI) requirements.
ITID-51241.priority: P1 upon confirmation of POS malware; card brands and acquiring banks require rapid containment and forensic engagement.
ITID-51241.escalation: Escalate immediately to PCI compliance, legal, and the acquiring bank/card brands per merchant agreement; engage a PCI Forensic Investigator (PFI) if required by the card brands.
indicators: Unusual process running on POS terminals with memory-scraping behavior
Outbound connections from POS network segment to unfamiliar external hosts
Spike in confirmed fraudulent card use traceable to a common merchant (a 'common point of purchase' identified by card networks)
vectors: Malware delivered via compromised remote access tool (e.g., vendor remote support software) into the POS environment
Lateral movement from corporate network into an inadequately segmented POS network
Malicious removable media plugged into a POS terminal
rootCauses: Inadequate network segmentation between POS and corporate/guest networks
Unencrypted card data in POS terminal memory (no point-to-point encryption)
Weak or shared remote access credentials for POS vendor support tools
controls: Point-to-point encryption (P2PE) of card data at the point of capture
Network segmentation isolating the POS environment (PCI DSS Requirement 1)
File integrity monitoring on POS terminals
ITID-51241.detection: Strong signal available via network segmentation monitoring, endpoint detection on POS terminals, and card-brand fraud alerts (common point of purchase analysis).
ITID-51241.response: Isolate affected POS terminals/segments, preserve forensic evidence, and engage a PFI per PCI DSS incident response requirements before card brand reporting deadlines.
metrics: Number of POS terminals confirmed infected
Card records potentially exposed
Time from infection to detection
ITID-51241.notes: T1056.001 is used per the payment-card breach MITRE mapping guidance for POS environments (keylogging/input-capture behavior of RAM-scraping malware).

playbook.name: Point-of-Sale (POS) Malware Skimming Payment Card Data
playbook.description: Malware installed on point-of-sale terminals or supporting infrastructure captured payment card data (track data/CVV) from transactions in real time.

steps.title: Detect POS malware and identify affected terminals/environment
steps.desc: Confirm the presence of memory-scraping or card-skimming malware on POS terminals or the POS network via EDR alerts, unusual outbound traffic, or card-brand/acquirer fraud-pattern alerts (common point of purchase, CPP).
steps.guidance: Card-brand CPP alerts are often the first external signal; correlate with internal EDR/network telemetry to confirm and scope.
steps.outcome: Confirmed malware presence and list of affected terminals/locations.
steps.abort: If no malware or anomalous card-data access is found despite the alert, document and close pending further monitoring.

steps.title: Determine transaction window and card data volume exposed
steps.desc: Establish the dwell time of the malware and estimate the number and range of transactions/cards potentially captured.
steps.guidance: Use malware timestamps, transaction logs, and network capture artifacts to bound the exposure window.
steps.outcome: A defined exposure window and estimated card count for PCI forensic reporting.

steps.title: Isolate and take affected POS terminals offline
steps.desc: Immediately remove infected POS terminals/systems from the network and, if necessary, switch to manual/offline payment processing to stop ongoing capture.
steps.guidance: Preserve terminal memory/disk images before remediation for the required PCI forensic investigation.
steps.outcome: No further card data is being captured by the malware.

steps.title: Engage a PCI Forensic Investigator (PFI) and notify the acquirer/card brands
steps.desc: Engage a PCI SSC-approved forensic investigator as required by the merchant agreement, and notify the acquiring bank and card brands per PCI-DSS incident response requirements.
steps.guidance: This is typically a contractual, non-optional obligation once card-data compromise is suspected — do not delay pending full internal investigation.
steps.outcome: PFI engaged and required notifications to acquirer/card brands made within contractual timeframes.

steps.title: Remove malware and remediate the infection vector across all POS systems
steps.desc: Eradicate the malware from all affected and at-risk terminals, and close the vector used for initial infection (e.g. remote access compromise, vulnerable third-party software, weak POS network segmentation).
steps.guidance: Coordinate remediation scope with the PFI's findings before reconnecting terminals to production.
steps.outcome: No malware remains and the infection vector is closed across the estate.

steps.title: Implement point-to-point encryption/tokenization and network segmentation hardening
steps.desc: Deploy or strengthen P2PE/tokenization so card data is never exposed in cleartext at the terminal, and enforce strict segmentation of the POS network from the general corporate network.
steps.outcome: Future malware on the POS network cannot access cleartext card data even if reinfected.

steps.title: Validate clean terminals and resume normal payment processing
steps.desc: Confirm with the PFI and internal validation that terminals are clean before returning to normal electronic payment processing.
steps.outcome: POS environment confirmed clean and fully operational.

steps.title: Complete PCI incident report and drive compliance remediation
steps.desc: Document the PFI's findings and remediation for the acquirer/card brands, and track required PCI-DSS compliance gaps closed as a result.
steps.outcome: Formal PCI incident report filed with tracked remediation actions.

ITID-51242.def: An incident in which an adversary injects malicious JavaScript into an e-commerce site's checkout or payment page (directly, or via a compromised third-party script/tag) to capture and exfiltrate payment card data entered by customers in real time.
ITID-51242.purpose: Captures card-not-present payment data theft via malicious JavaScript injected into an e-commerce checkout page (Magecart-style web skimming).
scopeIncludes: Direct compromise of e-commerce platform code to inject a skimmer script
Compromise of a third-party JavaScript library or tag manager loaded on the checkout page (supply-chain skimming)
Skimmer exfiltrating captured card data to an attacker-controlled domain
scopeExcludes: POS terminal malware for card-present transactions (POS Malware leaf)
Physical skimming hardware (Physical Card Skimming Device Breach leaf)
Breach at the payment processor/gateway itself rather than the merchant's page (Compromised Payment Processor leaf)
ITID-51242.severity: High; web skimmers can silently harvest card data from every checkout transaction until detected, often for weeks or months.
ITID-51242.priority: P1 upon confirmation of active skimmer code; requires immediate page takedown/remediation to stop ongoing card capture.
ITID-51242.escalation: Escalate to PCI compliance, e-commerce/web engineering, and legal immediately; notify the acquiring bank/card brands per merchant agreement.
indicators: Unrecognized or modified JavaScript on the checkout page
Outbound requests from customer browsers to an unfamiliar exfiltration domain during checkout
Content Security Policy (CSP) violation reports flagging unexpected script sources
Spike in card fraud traceable to purchases made on the site
vectors: Compromise of the e-commerce CMS/admin panel to inject skimmer code directly
Compromise of a third-party script (analytics, chat widget, ad tag) loaded on the checkout page
Exploitation of an outdated e-commerce platform plugin
rootCauses: Lack of Subresource Integrity (SRI) or CSP restricting third-party scripts on payment pages
